title: 3-Read Friday #57: Performance vs Learning, Cognitive Endurance, and Number Patterns
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 57 is a research-dense trio centred on cognitive science and one maths-specific activity. Barton first recommends Paul Kirschner's post distinguishing performance from learning, summarising it as explaining why the distinction matters and what teachers can do to avoid over-indexing on performance. He then highlights Doug Lemov's piece connecting attention and 'cognitive endurance' to reading instruction, tying it to his own long-running interest in students' lack of attention, and links the underlying NBER working paper directly for readers who want the primary source. His third pick is Sam Blatherwick's number-pattern activity designed to build curiosity about relationships between numbers. The issue closes with a plug for Barton's new 90-minute online CPD workshops rather than the usual newsletter-archive link.
points: Barton frames the Kirschner pick around the performance/learning distinction's practical payoff -- 'concrete things teachers can do to avoid putting all our eggs in the performance basket' -- rather than just the theory.
By linking directly to the underlying NBER working paper behind Lemov's post, Barton signals a habit of sending readers to primary research, not just secondhand commentary.
His description of his own 'obsession' with student attention (repeated across multiple issues) shows attention/engagement as one of the recurring throughlines of his curatorial judgment.

The pivot to promoting his own paid CPD workshops in the sign-off, replacing the usual newsletter-archive plug, marks a small but real shift in how Barton monetises the newsletter's audience going into 2025.
quotes: Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
Paul summarises the differences, explains why they matter, and suggests concrete things teachers can do to avoid putting all our eggs in the performance basket.
Long-time readers will know about my obsession with students' attention (or, more accurately, students' lack of attention).
Here, Doug shares his work on reading and a fascinating study about how cognitive endurance - the ability to remain focussed for long periods - can be built up through practice.
Sam shares a lovely activity to help students gain curiosity in numbers, patterns and relationships.
